Why My Mylapore Filter Coffee Has Better DevOps Than My Software Team

# Why My Mylapore Filter Coffee Has Better DevOps Than My Software Team

### In my house, the daily stand-up happens near the stove. Stakeholders are fully engaged. Feedback is immediate. Production outages are remembered for generations.

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

![Amaruvi Devanathan's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bq_i!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F357700fd-8e69-44fa-a5f8-000e6e26808a_1002x1002.jpeg)

I have spent more than thirty years in software.

I’ve survived Y2K.

I’ve survived ERP implementations.

I’ve survived digital transformation, cloud transformation, AI transformation, and several managers who believed transformation itself was a strategy.

And yet, every single morning, one ancient stainless-steel filter sitting in my kitchen continues to outperform every modern technology stack I have worked on.

I’m not even joking.

The filter has achieved what no startup, consultant, or Chief Transformation Officer has managed to achieve.

Consistent delivery.

Zero drama.

Excellent user satisfaction.

No PowerPoint.

The realization hit me one morning while I was making coffee.

Not drinking coffee.

Making coffee.

Because every true Tamil Brahmin knows there is a difference.

Anybody can drink coffee.

Making filter coffee is a sacred operating procedure handed down through generations of paatis who would never use the phrase “best practices” but somehow invented all of them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Requirements Gathering: The Most Dangerous Phase

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

People think software requirements are confusing.

Clearly they’ve never asked a Tamil Brahmin family how they like their coffee.

In my house, I have stakeholders.

One wants it “strong-aa.”

Another wants it “konjam less strong.”

One person wants more milk.

Another wants less milk.

One person wants sugar.

Another person has suddenly become health-conscious after watching three Instagram reels and wants palm jaggery.

One aunt insists coffee tasted better in 1987.

Nobody knows why.

Nobody can reproduce the environment.

Yet she remains firm.

In software, we call these changing requirements.

In Tamil households, we call them relatives.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sprint Planning Begins at 5:30 AM

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every morning starts with a backlog grooming session.

I open the coffee dabba.

First task:

Assess inventory.

Do we have enough powder?

Has somebody forgotten to buy milk?

Has someone finished the sugar and quietly returned the empty container to the shelf like a production bug being reassigned to another team?

Risk assessment is critical.

Coffee is not a beverage.

Coffee is infrastructure.

Failure is not an option.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Architecture Is Surprisingly Elegant

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Young software architects love complexity.

Microservices.

Containers.

Service meshes.

Event-driven architectures.

Twelve monitoring dashboards.

Three observability tools.

And somehow nobody knows why the login page is down.

Meanwhile, the filter coffee system architecture is astonishingly simple.

Top chamber.

Bottom chamber.

Gravity.

Done.

No Kubernetes.

No AI.

No blockchain-enabled coffee experience.

No monthly subscription.

Nobody asks me to scan a QR code before accessing my caffeine.

The user journey is refreshingly uncomplicated.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Build Process

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is where real engineering begins.

First comes the powder.

Now, this is not some random powder from a supermarket shelf.

Every Tamil Brahmin family has coffee powder preferences that resemble religious denominations.

There are factions.

There are loyalties.

There are blood feuds.

Families have been known to discuss coffee powder brands with more passion than national elections.

I carefully fill the filter.

Not too much.

Not too little.

Just enough.

This is essentially capacity planning.

Then comes the most satisfying moment.

Pouring hot water into the upper chamber.

The sound alone deserves its own Spotify playlist.

Then I close the lid.

And wait.

This is where software engineers struggle.

We have become addicted to speed.

Faster builds.

Faster deployments.

Faster releases.

Faster feedback.

Filter coffee laughs at our impatience.

The decoction drips at exactly the speed it wants.

Not the speed in your sprint commitment.

Not the speed promised to leadership.

Not the speed estimated in Jira.

The speed chosen by physics.

For once, gravity is the project manager.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Observability

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The modern software industry spends billions on observability.

Meanwhile, my paati could monitor an entire coffee system using only smell.

I have seen this woman sitting in another room.

The milk is on the stove.

The coffee is dripping.

The pressure cooker is whistling.

The TV is running.

Three grandchildren are fighting.

Yet somehow she suddenly shouts:

“Milk varudhu! Paathu!”

She has detected an incident before the incident occurred.

Datadog wishes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Quality Assurance

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Now comes testing.

I open the filter.

The decoction has arrived.

Dark.

Strong.

Glorious.

This is not a beverage.

This is intellectual property.

I take a tiny sniff.

Every Tamil household has this step.

Nobody documents it.

Nobody explains it.

But it happens.

We sniff.

We evaluate.

We make serious faces.

We pretend we are sommeliers at an international coffee conference.

“Hmmm.”

“Powder konjam different-aa irukku.”

“Last week batch better.”

The confidence with which completely unscientific conclusions are delivered is truly inspiring.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Integration Testing

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Next comes milk integration.

This is where systems fail.

Too much milk.

Coffee disappears.

Too little milk.

Entire family starts discussing acidity.

Wrong temperature.

Stakeholder dissatisfaction.

This is exactly like software integration.

Everything works beautifully in isolation.

The moment components meet each other, chaos begins.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Production Deployment

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Now comes deployment.

I perform the sacred davara-tumbler transfer.

Back and forth.

Back and forth.

Back and forth.

Every Tamil kid has watched this process with the same awe that Americans reserve for rocket launches.

The foam rises.

The aroma spreads.

At this point something magical happens.

People appear.

Nobody was around five minutes ago.

Suddenly:

“Coffee ready-aa?”

My husband.

My daughter.

Random visiting relative.

Neighbour auntie.

Everybody materializes.

Filter coffee is basically an event-driven architecture.

The event is aroma.

The consumers subscribe automatically.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## User Acceptance Testing

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is the most dangerous phase.

Because the users are now involved.

Software customers usually file tickets.

Tamil relatives provide verbal feedback.

Immediately.

Without moderation.

Without fear.

Without legal review.

One sip.

Then:

“Sema.”

Or:

“Konjam strong-aa irukkalam.”

Or the most terrifying phrase in Tamil family history:

“Yesterday better.”

There is no recovering from that.

The release has failed.

Postmortem will be conducted for the next six months.

## Legacy Systems

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every software company has legacy code.

Nobody understands it.

Nobody wants to touch it.

Everybody fears it.

My mother’s coffee procedure is exactly like that.

There are rules.

Unwritten rules.

Mystical rules.

Rules nobody can explain.

Why should the spoon be that spoon?

Why should the filter face east while drying?

Why must the powder be pressed exactly that much?

Nobody knows.

The answer is always:

“Appadi than pannuvom.”

Which is Tamil for:

“Please stop asking architectural questions.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Artificial Intelligence Meets Mylapore

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Everyone is excited about AI now.

AI will write code.

AI will create art.

AI will replace jobs.

Fine.

Maybe.

But can AI identify the exact moment when decoction strength is perfect?

Can it recognize from one sip that milk came from a different packet?

Can it predict which auntie is about to ask whether you have gained weight?

Can it estimate how much extra coffee is needed because one cousin said she’s “just dropping by for five minutes”?

Tamil Brahmin women have been doing predictive analytics for decades.

Without GPUs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Women in Tech Will Understand This

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every woman reading this knows exactly what happens next.

You finish making coffee.

You hand everyone their tumblers.

You sit down.

Finally.

You take your first sip.

Slack notification.

Phone rings.

School WhatsApp message.

Grocery reminder.

Family group discussing somebody’s engagement.

Office Teams alert marked “urgent.”

Congratulations.

Your production environment is live.

Again.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Greatest Lesson Filter Coffee Taught Me

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After decades in software, I have learned that the best systems are not necessarily the most innovative.

They’re the most reliable.

Nobody writes LinkedIn posts about reliable things.

Nobody creates TED Talks about consistency.

Nobody raises venture capital for predictability.

Yet every morning, millions of South Indians place their faith in a humble steel filter.

And the filter delivers.

No pivot.

No disruption.

No AI roadmap.

No quarterly strategy offsite.

Just excellent output.

Every single day.

Meanwhile my software applications need three patches, two hotfixes, and one emergency rollback before breakfast.

So these days, whenever somebody asks me about engineering excellence, I don’t think about Silicon Valley.

I think about my paati.

Standing in a madisar.

Managing stakeholders.

Handling production load.

Running quality assurance.

Maintaining legacy systems.

Performing predictive analytics.

And delivering flawless releases before sunrise.

Frankly, if my software teams operated like Mylapore women making filter coffee, we’d probably achieve 99.999% uptime.

And a lot fewer meetings.

☕️

*In my office, we run unit tests.*

*At home, we run decoction tests.*

*The decoction continues to outperform the software.*
